The Two Sons

One son changes his mind; another never turns agreement into action. Jesus makes the difference between a response and its appearance clear.

Open study →

The Barren Fig Tree

The gardener asks for time to dig and nourish. Jesus places urgent repentance beside a patient opportunity to bear fruit.

Open study →

The Budding Fig Tree

New leaves tell an observer something about the season. Jesus invites discernment while leaving the day and hour unknown.

Open study →

The Doorkeeper

The master leaves work for each servant and watchfulness for the porter. The unknown hour does not erase their present responsibility.

Open study →

The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant

Someone else's daily bread is placed in a servant's care. The master's absence reveals how that trust will be used.

Open study →

The Talents

Different amounts are entrusted to different servants. The returning master asks what each has done with the responsibility received.

Open study →

The Ten Pounds or Minas

People expect the kingdom immediately; Jesus tells of work during an absence. Luke's account joins waiting with stewardship.

Open study →

The Ten Virgins

All ten wait and all ten sleep, but their preparation differs. The midnight announcement reveals what they have brought to the waiting.

Open study →

Servants Waiting for Their Lord

The lamps are ready and the door can be opened. Jesus pictures waiting that is attentive, then surprises His hearers with the master's welcome.

The Sower

The same seed meets different ground. Jesus explains what can prevent His word from taking root and what makes room for enduring fruit.

The Seed Growing Secretly

Between sowing and harvest, growth unfolds beyond the farmer's control. Mark's brief parable invites patient attention to God's kingdom.

Open study →

The Mustard Seed

Jesus places a small seed beside the branches it becomes. The kingdom's beginning does not reveal the full reach of its growth.

Open study →

The Leaven

A woman's work with meal becomes a picture of the kingdom. The change reaches throughout the batch before the story ends.

A lamp, a broom, and a careful search show that one missing coin still matters. Its recovery calls neighbors into the joy.

The Laborers in the Vineyard

Equal generosity becomes difficult for workers who expected more. The vineyard story examines gratitude, comparison, and resentment.

Peter asks about forgiveness. The enormous forgiven debt throws the servant's refusal of mercy into sharp relief; forgiveness does not require returning to

The Two Debtors

A brief story changes the conversation at Simon's table. Forgiveness invites him to look again at a woman whose love he has overlooked.

The Pharisee and the Publican

Two people pray, but their posture toward God and others differs. Jesus invites a searching look at comparison, confidence, and mercy.

Open study →

Choosing the Lower Place

At a meal, Jesus notices the places people choose. His teaching moves from seeking honor to offering generous welcome.

Open study →

The Great Supper

The supper is ready, but the first invitees excuse themselves. The widening invitation brings overlooked people toward a place at the table.

Open study →

The Wedding of the King's Son

The wedding invitation is refused, widened, and finally answered. Matthew's account asks readers to take both the welcome and their response seriousl

Jesus identifies Himself as the door and good shepherd who lays down His life. The Bible Dictionary calls this an allegory; Harmony uses the broader

The True Vine and the Branches

A branch lives through its connection to the vine. Jesus joins abiding, love, obedience, and fruitfulness in His farewell teaching.

Open study →

The Hen Gathering Her Chicks

Jesus laments over Jerusalem with a picture of protective gathering. Preserve both His invitation and the sorrow of refusal.

Open study →

The Sheep and the Goats

The Son of Man identifies care for people in need with service to Him. This is an extended judgment scene with a shepherd comparison, commonly included amo

The Good Samaritan

A question about who counts as a neighbor becomes a story about acting as one. Follow the mercy that begins on the road and continues at the inn.

Open study →

The Rich Man and Lazarus

A suffering man lies at a rich man's gate. The account moves from that ignored need toward a call to hear the word already given.

Open study →

The Rich Fool

A rich harvest promises the owner many comfortable years. The story asks what possessions can and cannot secure.

Open study →

Birds and Lilies

Jesus draws attention to creatures and flowers while speaking of daily needs. The invitation is to seek the kingdom with trust in the Father's care.

Open study →

A Parent's Good Gifts

A child's request for food becomes a way to think about prayer. Jesus directs trust toward the Father's goodness.

Open study →

The Friend at Midnight

An unexpected guest leaves a host asking for bread in the night. Jesus places persistence beside the Father's goodness.

Open study →

The Persistent Widow and the Judge

A widow keeps bringing a claim that a judge dismisses. Jesus directs weary hearers toward continued prayer and the goodness of God.

The New Patch

Read within the question about fasting. Jesus describes the damage caused by joining an unshrunk patch to an old garment.

New Wine and Wineskins

Wine needs a vessel able to receive it. Jesus uses this ordinary image to help His hearers consider the significance of His presence and teaching.

The bridegroom's presence makes the occasion one of joy. Jesus answers a question about fasting through the significance of His own mission.

The Strong Man

Jesus answers the charge that His deliverance comes from Satan. Luke develops the image of a stronger conqueror; this is not a lesson endorsing robbery.

A Divided Kingdom and House

An accusation fails to explain the deliverance before the hearers. Jesus exposes the contradiction through a kingdom and household divided.

The Returning Unclean Spirit

An emptied house is not the same as a renewed life. This unsettling comparison asks for a response deeper than a temporary change.

Open study →

The Householder and the Thief

The unexpected arrival calls for readiness. The comparison concerns timing, not a claim that the Lord shares a thief's character.

Open study →

Settling with an Adversary

The legal journey illustrates urgency. Offer spiritual reflection without turning it into individualized legal advice.

Open study →

The Sheep in the Pit

A rescue question supports doing good on the Sabbath. Luke uses an ass or ox in a related scene; do not label the two identical stories.

Open study →

The Tower Builder

Counting construction costs illustrates the serious commitment of discipleship. Read the short picture within Jesus' surrounding teaching.

Open study →

The King Considering War

A king considers whether his forces are sufficient and seeks peace. This companion comparison concerns counting the cost of discipleship, not an endorseme

The Unjust Steward

The steward prepares for losing his position. Distinguish commendation of shrewd preparation from approval of dishonesty, then read Jesus' teaching on faithfuln

The Servant's Duty

Ordinary service challenges a sense of entitlement. Do not use the language of an unprofitable servant to deny a person's worth or justify exploitation.

The lamp is meant to give light. Compare the different surrounding teachings about witness, hearing, and inward light rather than merging every setting.

Jesus compares inconsistent reactions to John and Himself with children who reject both kinds of music. Read the accusations in the following verses.

After asking whether the disciples understand, Jesus speaks of a trained scribe bringing out treasures new and old. Treat this as a compact concluding c

The Blind Leading the Blind

Luke explicitly introduces a parable. Spiritual guidance is the subject; do not turn blindness into a moral judgment about people with disabilities.

The Mote and the Beam

Exaggerated imagery exposes hypocrisy before correction of another. An application should invite self-examination.

Open study →

A Tree and Its Fruit

Fruit reveals character in sayings about teachers, speech, and conduct. Keep each setting visible.

Open study →

Salt of the Earth

The shared salt image occurs in different teaching contexts. It is a related comparison rather than a narrated story.

Open study →

The Wheat and the Tares

Read Jesus' explanation after the story. The servants are restrained from uprooting wheat; judgment belongs to the appointed harvest.

Open study →

The Hidden Treasure

Joy over discovered treasure leads to wholehearted action. Keep the narrative brief instead of supplying an invented biography.

Open study →

The Pearl of Great Price

A merchant recognizes one pearl's value and sells all to obtain it. Study beside the treasure while preserving the difference between seeking and finding.

The Fishing Net

The catch is gathered and sorted. Jesus explicitly connects the separation with judgment; the text does not authorize us to decide another person's final standing.

The Grain of Wheat

Jesus uses a dying seed when speaking of His approaching glorification and following Him.

Open study →

The Closed Door

A shut door answers a question about salvation. Familiarity is not the same as responding to the Lord.

Open study →

Sorrow Turning to Joy

Childbirth illustrates sorrow giving way to joy in the farewell discourse. It is an analogy, not a prediction about an individual pregnancy.
